extracted.intended_audience: OSHA rulemaking stakeholders: employers, workers, occupational health professionals, regulators, and public commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes peer‑reviewed and surveillance evidence on occupational heat-related illnesses (heat cramps, heat rash, heat edema, kidney stones, acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease), including definitions, physiological mechanisms, incidence data, case identification, treatment, recovery, and study limitations to support OSHA rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat cramps — definition and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat cramps (sometimes called exercise-associated muscle cramps (EAMCs) but distinct because they only occur in hot conditions) are painful muscle cramps associated with profuse sweating and electrolyte depletion (e.g., sodium, potassium, calcium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism proposed: electrolyte depletion exacerbates muscle fatigue; U.S. Army posits intracellular calcium increases via reduction in sodium gradient stimulating actin-myosin interactions. Cited prevalence in worker and athlete studies (e.g., 25–35% self-reported in farmworker samples; 70% of exertional heat illness in collegiate football in August).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat cramps — treatment and work-return considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment includes electrolyte-containing (isotonic) fluid replacement, stretching, massage, and in some cases sodium replacement or magnesium replacement (IV) for severe cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACSM recommends rest, prolonged stretching, oral sodium chloride ingestion or IV normal saline in severe cases. NIOSH recommends medical attention if worker has heart problems, is on a low sodium diet, or if cramps do not subside within 1 hour. If treated early, individuals may return to activity after cramps subside; military guidelines sometimes recommend light workload the next day and limited workload following day and avoidance of strenuous exercise for several days in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat rash (miliaria rubra) — definition and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH defines heat rash as 'a skin irritation caused by excessive sweating during hot, humid weather' (also called miliaria rubra or prickly heat), presenting as red clusters of pimples or small blisters with itching/prickly sensations, typically in areas where clothing is restrictive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat rash can last several days, may become infected if untreated, and in some cases lead to hypohidrosis (reduced ability to sweat) that impairs thermoregulation for weeks. Clothing (occlusive or sweat-soaked fabrics, chemical additives) can worsen severity; multiple prevalence estimates from worker studies are reported but vary by methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat rash — treatment and workplace guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most cases can be self-treated; keep affected area dry and cool, move to a cooler/less humid environment, avoid tight-fitting clothing, avoid oil-based ointments; powder may be used for relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt care reduces infection risk; severe cases can impair ability to work and may require time away to allow area to heal (3–4 weeks for heat intolerance to subside in some cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat edema — definition and mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat edema is swelling of soft tissues (typically lower extremities and hands) associated with heat exposure and vasodilation; blood pools in gravity-dependent areas causing fluid seepage under the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers who sit/stand for prolonged periods or who are not acclimatized may be at higher risk. Surveillance is limited; prevalence estimates in some agricultural/sugarcane worker studies are reported but methods vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat edema — treatment and return-to-work guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most cases self‑treatable; move out of heat and elevate swollen area. Diuretics are not typically recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symptoms can last days; proper acclimatization reduces recurrence likelihood. Severe swelling may impede ability to perform job tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kidney stones — definition, symptoms, risk factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Kidney stones are hard mineral objects forming in the kidney; symptoms include sharp pain (back/side/abdomen/groin), hematuria, urinary urgency, nausea/vomiting, fever/chills. Risk factors include male sex, family history, prior stones, low fluid intake, certain medical conditions, sugary beverages, and occupational heat exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological mechanism: heat-induced sweating and dehydration reduce urine volume, increase vasopressin, concentrate insoluble salts (e.g., calcium oxalate) leading to crystal formation. Epidemiologic studies (indoor/outdoor workers internationally) support heat exposure as a risk factor. Treatment depends on size/location; small stones may pass with hydration and analgesics, larger stones may require lithotripsy, ureteroscopy, or percutaneous nephrolithotomy. Work absence is common (one study: average 19 hours missed per treated person). Recurrent stones increase risk of CKD and ESRD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acute kidney injury (AKI) — definition and categories
rubrics_metrics.description: AKI is an abrupt decline in kidney function over a short period (e.g., days). Categories distinguish the location of cause: prerenal (reduced renal perfusion), intrarenal (injury to glomeruli/tubules/interstitium), and postrenal (urinary obstruction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prerenal AKI may result from heat-induced sweating and reduced circulating volume; intrarenal causes include nephrotoxins or rhabdomyolysis; postrenal causes (e.g., stones) are less relevant except where stones occur. Severity and reversibility vary by cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: AKI — case identification and biomarkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Serum creatinine is commonly used to estimate GFR and identify AKI; multiple criteria exist for defining AKI, such as the KDIGO criteria (based on increases in serum creatinine over hours or days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: serum creatinine can be affected by exercise (increased production) and may be unreliable for short‑term GFR changes. Alternative/supplementary biomarkers (e.g., neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin, NGAL) are increasingly used and may be more specific to AKI. The document cites use of both serum creatinine and NGAL in experimental and observational studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: AKI — mechanisms linking heat exposure to injury
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed mechanisms include: (1) elevated core temperature directly injuring renal tissue; (2) subclinical rhabdomyolysis causing tubular necrosis via myoglobin precipitation; (3) reduced renal blood flow/ischemia from hypovolemia; (4) physiologic pathway activation (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, polyol-fructokinase) causing oxidative stress and inflammation; (5) urate crystal-induced injury and increased reabsorption of nephrotoxicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence comes from experimental, animal, and observational studies. Magnitude of kidney injury may be proportional to magnitude of heat strain; limiting hyperthermia/dehydration reduces AKI biomarker elevations (trials with water/cooling interventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: AKI — epidemiologic and surveillance evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Observational studies and OSHA databases document AKI associated with occupational heat: experimental increases in serum creatinine/NGAL with heat strain; field studies reporting post-shift AKI incidences (e.g., 12.3%, 33% in cohort studies); OSHA OOMN and SIR database identified cases using serum creatinine elevations meeting KDIGO and heat-related codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations include reliance on serum creatinine, short measurement windows, inability in some studies to distinguish prerenal from intrarenal causes, and potential confounding. Nonetheless, both experimental and observational literatures suggest occupational heat exposure causes AKI.

rubrics_metrics.name: AKI — treatment, recovery, and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Severity ranges from asymptomatic biomarker elevations to irreversible injury. Some AKI biomarkers return to baseline quickly; intrarenal AKI may require medication or dialysis. Recurrent AKI can lead to chronic kidney disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat stroke-related AKI can be severe and potentially fatal. Recovery timelines and treatment depend on cause and severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) — definition and diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: CKD is a progressive decline in kidney function over months to years, typically asymptomatic until late stages. Diagnosis typically requires multiple blood and urine tests over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common diagnostic threshold: estimated GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m2 for at least 3 months (other indicators include high albumin-to-creatinine ratio). Researchers propose CKD may develop from repeated heat-related AKI events, though causation is not definitively established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study and surveillance limitations — comparability and case definition concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Many studies rely on self-reported symptoms or differing diagnostic methods; differences in study methodologies and populations limit comparability across studies and to U.S. populations. Use of serum creatinine has limitations for short-term AKI detection; short measurement spans may miss true GFR declines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes limitations when interpreting prevalence/incidence estimates; encouraging use of validated biomarkers (e.g., NGAL) and standardized case definitions (e.g., KDIGO) where possible. Observational findings should be interpreted in light of potential confounding and inability to definitively classify AKI etiology in some datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency classification and nomenclature of heat-related illnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: NIOSH, the U.S. Army, and the U.S. Navy classify conditions like heat cramps, heat rash, and heat edema as heat-related illnesses; the page distinguishes related terms (e.g., exercise-associated muscle cramps versus heat cramps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using consistent nomenclature (e.g., specifying whether cramps are heat-specific vs exercise-associated) and recognizing agency classifications aids in surveillance, diagnosis, and regulatory discussion.
